newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-HENMAN KEEPS BRITISH FLAG FLYING.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HENMAN KEEPS BRITISH FLAG FLYING.

text.p: Tim Henman improved Britain's chances of celebrating a first Wimbledon men's champion for 61 years on Wednesday as Richard Krajicek's reign shuddered to an abrupt halt on Centre Court.
Henman needed only 36 minutes to wrap up a superb 7-6 6-7 7-6 6-4 victory over the Dutchman, ensuring two British representatives in the last eight for the first time since 1961.

Another ex-champion, Germany's Michael Stich, now stands between Henman and a first appearance in a Wimbledon semifinal, but the style and confidence which oozed from the 22-year-old suggested anything is now possible.
"I feel very confident," admitted Henman. "For the sustained quality of tennis this is the best match I've ever played.
"To beat the Wimbledon champion I think you've got to be playing pretty well and that's exactly what I've done."
Resuming with a two sets to one lead after bad light had intervened the previous evening, Henman grasped the initiative by winning 12 out of 13 points to soar from 2-1 down to 4-2 ahead.

He did allow Krajicek one break point opportunity in the next game but salvaged the situation with an ace and completed victory in two hours 52 minutes in front of a Centre Court crowd which included former American president George Bush.

There is a distinct possibility of him meeting compatriot Greg Rusedski, who faces France's Cedric Pioline in the last eight, in an all-British semifinal but Henman remains wary of the experienced Stich.

"He's announced he's retiring this year and I think it's probably taken a big weight off his shoulders. He seems to be very relaxed and grass is obviously a surface which suits his game...I think it will be a very similar match to the Krajicek one."

The crowds are obviously willing Henman to become the first British men's champion since Fred Perry in 1936, even if they are not exhibiting quite the same levels of patriotic fervour seen on 'People's Sunday' last weekend when he beat American Jonathan Stark.
"I think both Greg and I are riding a wave of people's euphoria and we'd both like it to continue.

"You have to try and stay in control of your emotions, because there are 14,000 people who aren't in control of theirs. I was very calm throughout the match and once I had broken him, I wasn't going to let my opportunity go."
Krajicek was disappointed with his own display -- "I couldn't believe I'd play worse than yesterday but I did. He didn't make any mistakes" -- but did not attach any blame to the partisan crowd.
"They are very noisy but as soon as the point starts you can hear a pin drop. I think that shows a lot of respect for the players."
He had been keen for the match to be stopped earlier the previous evening, and revealed he had asked tournament referee Alan Mills to intervene at the end of the second set.
"It must have been a long way from the referee's office to the court, because it took him seven games to get there," commented Krajicek with heavy irony.
The Dutchman will also depart Wimbledon with one small detail stored away for the future.
"The one thing I do know is that I'm not going to name my kid Tim. I hate that name," he smiled.

Many British parents-to-be will doubtless disagree if Henman does go all the way. He is already the first British man to defeat a defending Wimbledon champion since Roger Taylor beat Rod Laver in 1970.
